KS-2025-HB2006.s: The bill would move certain Department of Corrections security officers into the Kansas Police and Firemen's Retirement System, starting July 1, 2025. It would require employee and employer contributions for those members. It would also let eligible officers buy retirement credit for past security officer service under KPERS, either through ongoing payments or a lump sum.

KS-2025-HB2009.s: The bill would make abortion illegal unless it is needed to save the pregnant woman’s life in a medical emergency. It would also let private people file civil lawsuits against those who perform, help with, or pay for a banned abortion. The measure would mainly affect abortion providers, drug sellers, and others who help with the procedure.

KS-2025-HB2011.s: The bill would lower the school district property tax rate in Kansas and set a new way to adjust it in later school years so it brings in the same revenue as the 2025-2026 school year. It would affect school districts and property owners, including owners of residential property. The bill also would send the tax money to the state school district finance fund and would take effect when published in the statute book.

KS-2025-HB2029.s: The bill would name a stretch of K-5 highway in Wyandotte County as the Representative Marvin S Robinson II memorial highway. It would also change the law for part of Interstate 635 to update the Harry Darby memorial highway route and keep the marker signs for both highways. The act would take effect after it is published in the statute book.

KS-2025-HB2043.s: This bill would let people file a protest petition to challenge some increases in property tax revenue. It would also keep reimbursements from the taxpayer notification costs fund going for five more years.

KS-2025-HB2044.s: The bill would require insurance third-party administrators to keep separate fiduciary accounts for each payor and keep clear records of money in and out for each one. It would also require them to tell the insurance commissioner if they file for bankruptcy under federal Chapter 9 or Chapter 11. It would change notice and fee disclosure rules for covered people and payors.

KS-2025-HB2065.s: The bill would set rules for picking Kansas delegates to a U.S. Constitution amendment convention called under Article V. It would say who appoints the delegates, how they can be recalled, and what limits they must follow when voting. It would also set pay for their travel and expenses and make it a felony to vote for an unauthorized amendment.

KS-2025-HB2128.s: The bill would let the insurance commissioner pick and announce which NAIC instructions, calculations, and documents will apply for the next calendar year, and have that notice published in the Kansas Register. It would also let certain life insurers use health financial reports in some cases. The bill would update Kansas insurance rules to match parts of a national model law on group capital calculations and liquidity stress testing for insurance holding companies.

KS-2025-HB2131.s: The bill would require prosecutors in criminal cases to tell the defense when they plan to use testimony from a jailhouse witness, and to share key details about that witness’s past, deals, and any benefits tied to the testimony. It would also require each prosecutor’s office to keep a record of these cases and send that information to the Kansas Bureau of Investigation for a statewide database. If a jailhouse witness got a benefit for testifying, the prosecutor would also have to notify the victim tied to the case.

KS-2025-HB2161.s: The bill would give a Kansas income tax credit to retail dealers and distributors that sell biodiesel or renewable diesel blends for motor fuel. The credit would be 5 cents per gallon for taxable years 2026 through 2031, with a $5 million cap each year, and any unused credit could be carried forward for up to five years. It died in committee.

KS-2025-HB2205.s: The bill would ban people from lobbying for or being paid to lobby for certain foreign governments, foreign political parties, or related clients. It would let the attorney general file civil lawsuits against violators. The bill also sets civil penalties of up to $25,000 for a first violation, $100,000 for a second, and $150,000 for later violations.

KS-2025-HB2220.s: The bill would let city officials lower the speed limit in city home areas from 30 miles per hour to 25 miles per hour without doing an engineering and traffic study. It would affect local governments with control over those areas and drivers in them. The bill also included rules for other speed-limit changes under state traffic law.

KS-2025-HB2285.s: The bill would change the state definition of lead-based paint under Kansas’s lead poisoning prevention law for homes. It would count paint with lead at or above 0.009% by weight, or the lower level set by federal law, and would apply to people and businesses covered by that law.

KS-2025-HB2293.s: The bill would bar state and local government agencies from buying drones or drone parts if the key parts were made in a country of concern or by a foreign principal, unless narrow safety and security exceptions are met. It would also stop state agencies from signing contracts for finished goods or services from a foreign principal, with some exceptions for certain deals tied to U.S. national security review. The limits would not apply to contracts already entered into before July 1, 2025, and the act would take effect when published in the statute book.

KS-2025-HB2351.s: The bill would change Kansas law on arbitration in insurance contracts. For insurance contracts entered into or renewed after July 1, 2025, clauses that require appraisal or arbitration would not be valid, except for contracts between insurance companies, including reinsurance. It would also let a court decide if an agreement to arbitrate exists or applies.

KS-2025-HB2365.s: It would add and remove certain drugs in controlled substance schedules I, III, and IV and update the criminal code’s definition of fentanyl-related controlled substances.

KS-2025-HB2377.s: The bill would keep the way countywide retailers' sales tax is shared between counties and cities based on property tax levy amounts, rather than changing that formula now. It also keeps the current split for some of the money by population. The bill would apply in Kansas and was set to take effect when published in the statute book.

KS-2025-HB2386.s: The bill would update the income rules for Kansas’s children’s health insurance program. It would affect children and families who apply for or get coverage through that program, which is run by the Department of Health and Environment. The program’s eligibility would still depend on household income and available state and federal funds.

KS-2025-HB2400.s: The bill would add trail rides to the list of ranching activities that can count as agritourism. It would also let land used for that kind of activity be valued as agricultural land for property tax purposes. The change would affect ranches and other property used for registered agritourism activities.

KS-2025-HB2412.s: The bill would increase the criminal penalties for endangering a child and aggravated endangering a child when the child is under 6 years old. It would also require any prison sentence for aggravated child endangerment to be served at the same time as no other sentence, but one after the other, and it would take effect after publication in the state law book.

KS-2025-HB2417.s: The bill would let the state bank commissioner revoke a fiduciary financial institution charter if the institution does not follow the law or rules for it. Before the revocation becomes final, a majority of the legislative coordinating council would have to approve it. It would affect fiduciary financial institutions in Kansas.

KS-2025-HB2418.s: The bill would bar the state bank commissioner or any other state agency from acting as a receiver for a technology-enabled fiduciary financial institution if it becomes insolvent or files for bankruptcy. It would affect these financial institutions and state agencies that handle failed firms. The bill would also add this rule to the state law on technology-enabled fiduciary financial institutions.

KS-2025-HB2473.s: The bill would require anyone giving consent for a marriage to be at least 18 years old and would remove the current exceptions that allow younger people to marry with consent. It would affect marriage licenses and the people who can approve them in Kansas. The bill died in committee and did not become law.

KS-2025-HB2569.s: It would require court challenges to state election laws with statewide effect to be filed in the Shawnee County district court, and cases filed elsewhere would be moved there. It also included a possible change to limit advance voting if a court blocked the signature check rule. The governor vetoed the bill, and the veto was sustained.

KS-2025-HB2597.s: The bill would give Kansas employees paid sick leave. It would let workers earn at least 2 hours for every 30 hours worked, up to 40 hours a year, starting January 1, 2027, and it would set rules for when the leave could be used. The bill also says the state labor secretary would write rules to carry it out. It died in committee.

KS-2025-HB2598.s: The bill would create a paid family leave program in Kansas for covered workers and some self-employed people who choose to join. It would let eligible people take paid leave to bond with a new child, care for a family member with a serious health condition, recover from their own serious health condition, or handle certain military family needs. The program would start paying benefits on July 1, 2027, and would set up a state fund for the leave payments. Employers would also have to give notice and handle payroll deductions for the premium that helps pay for the program.

KS-2025-HB2600.s: The bill would create the Affordable Healthcare for Kansans program and have the Kansas Department of Health and Environment run it. It would expand Medicaid, called medical assistance here, for adults under 65 who are not pregnant and whose income is at or below 138% of the federal poverty level. The new eligibility would start on January 1, 2027.

KS-2025-HB2620.s: The bill would raise the amount of the Kansas earned income tax credit that eligible resident individuals can claim. It would keep the rule that any credit above the tax owed is refunded to the taxpayer. The change would affect Kansas residents who qualify for the credit.

KS-2025-HB2651.s: The bill would change Kansas rules on paternity acknowledgments, which are signed forms that say who a child’s father is. It would let a person challenge one later in cases of fraud, duress, or a material mistake of fact, and it says certain genetic test results count as that kind of mistake. It would also require courts to consider a child’s best interests before ending an acknowledgment in some cases. The act would take effect when published in the statute book.

KS-2025-HB2656.s: The bill would create a state program for school districts to get money back for certain school breakfasts and lunches served to public school students. The state board of education would run the program, and districts would have to apply to take part. Participating districts would have to offer the meals at no cost to students, up to one breakfast and one lunch per school day.

KS-2025-HB2670.s: The bill would bar some video streaming services that reach Kansas users from running commercial ads with louder audio than the main video. It would apply to services that deliver video over the internet, but not to cable, broadcast TV, or services with no commercial ads. The rule would take effect after the act is published in the state statute book.

KS-2025-HB2679.s: The bill would create rules for adult-use cannabis in Kansas. It would set up licensing and regulation for growing, making, moving, having, and selling cannabis, and it would set fines and penalties for breaking the rules. It would also provide exceptions from some drug crimes, require expungement of cannabis-related charges, and add an excise tax to help fund child care, economic development, mental health, low-cost housing, and property tax rebates.

KS-2025-HB2692.s: The bill would set conduct rules for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Kansas. It would bar face coverings, require ID and clearly marked vehicles, require judicial search warrants for some searches and raids, and set a minimum training level. It would also forbid raids at schools, places of worship, daycare centers, hospitals, and courts without a warrant, and it would ban door-to-door raids in homes and apartments.

KS-2025-HB2707.s: The bill would change Kansas abuse protection rules to count threats or harm to a pet as abuse when done to control, punish, scare, or upset another person. It would also let courts include orders about pets in protection orders, including who has custody of a pet and keeping a person from harming or killing a pet. The changes would affect people seeking or facing protection from abuse orders, especially in households or dating relationships.

KS-2025-HB2731.s: The act requires the Kansas children and families secretary to contract with the office of the inspector general by January 1, 2027, to create a fraud detection unit for the food assistance program. The unit would detect, investigate, and help prosecute fraud, and the department would not use other workers or contractors for that work after that date.

KS-2025-HB2745.s: The bill would let voters approve some local property tax revenue increases for the next year, and it would set a ballot question for that vote. It would also create a property tax relief fund, with $60 million moved from the state general fund each year on July 15, rising by 2% starting in 2027, and send money to eligible counties for services like roads, law enforcement, elections, and public health and safety. Counties that hold the election would not get a payment from the fund. It would also keep the taxpayer notification costs fund in place for five more years.

KS-2025-HB2763.s: The bill would let Kansas join an interstate licensure compact for athletic trainers. It would let licensed athletic trainers in member states practice in other member states under set rules, while state licensing boards keep their role in licensing and discipline. It also sets shared rules for background checks, complaints, and sharing license and investigation info among member states.

KS-2025-HCR5006.s: The resolution would ask Kansas voters to amend the state bill of rights on the right to bear arms. It would say that right is a natural and fundamental right, and that it includes ammunition, firearm accessories, and firearm parts. Any limits on that right would have to meet the strict scrutiny standard, a very high legal test.

KS-2025-HCR5034.s: Would ask Kansas voters to amend the state constitution to create a freedom from taxes fund and a temporary review board. The board would review state tax exemptions and could approve or remove them. The proposal also would phase out motor vehicle property taxes and fees, certain property taxes, and state income and privilege taxes.

KS-2025-HR6028.s: The resolution would condemn the presence and practices of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and its related agencies, and honor people who died because of ICE enforcement actions or while in ICE custody. It would also call for an independent audit of ICE’s training, oversight, use-of-force rules, detention conditions, and accountability, with the findings released to the public. A copy would be sent to Kansas’s congressional delegation and some House members.

KS-2025-HR6030.s: The resolution would express support for Israel and say that Judea and Samaria are part of the land of Israel. It would also tell state agencies not to use the term “West Bank” in official government materials. The measure died in committee before becoming law.

KS-2025-SB101.s: The bill would have the attorney general appoint a statewide D.A.R.E. educator, with extra staff if money is available. The educator would teach drug abuse lessons in public elementary and secondary schools using an attorney general-approved curriculum that includes fentanyl and other opioid drugs. The educator would also report each year to lawmakers on curriculum changes and the schools served. If passed, the act would take effect after publication in the statute book.

KS-2025-SB132.s: Would change child care rules by lowering some license fees and training requirements for day care facilities, child care homes, and child care centers. It would also let day care license holders ask for a temporary waiver of some state rules and let the health and environment secretary run pilot programs to grow child care supply. The bill would move some child care programs to the Kansas office of early childhood and split licensing duties between that office and the health and environment department.

KS-2025-SB167.s: The bill would stop electric utilities from charging ratepayers for the costs of building, running, owning, or maintaining electric vehicle charging stations. It would require utilities that offer charging service to do that work through a separate private business and to treat private charging providers the same in fees and terms. It would also require utilities to set special charging rate plans, including a plan for direct-current fast charging, and to file or publish those plans by October 1, 2025, if they are approved or not under state commission control.

KS-2025-SB236.s: The bill would let adults who were abused or neglected as children get records tied to confirmed reports or investigations of that abuse or neglect. It would affect those adult survivors and the agencies that keep these records. The bill also says the records must not include the name of the person who made the report.

KS-2025-SB300.s: The bill would bar the state bank commissioner or any other state agency from acting as receiver for a technology-enabled fiduciary financial institution if it becomes insolvent or files bankruptcy. It also updates the law for these firms by adding rules and definitions, including what counts as insolvency, and it would take effect after publication in the statute book.

KS-2025-SB301.s: The bill would let the state bank commissioner revoke a technology-enabled fiduciary financial institution charter if the institution fails to follow the law or its rules. The revocation would not be final unless a majority of the legislative coordinating council approves it, and the institution could appeal to that council.

KS-2025-SB302.s: School districts and accredited nonpublic schools would have to set rules that stop students from using personal electronic devices during instructional time. It would also bar school employees from using social media to privately or directly contact students for official school purposes, with some exceptions and an option for approved school accounts. Schools would have to adopt these rules and report that they did so by September 1, 2026; virtual schools would not be covered.

KS-2025-SB304.s: The bill would require the state vital records office to send certain birth data to the state treasurer so the treasurer can mail information about savings accounts to families. It covers children born in Kansas, including those born before July 1, 2026 if they are still eligible, and children born on or after that date within 90 days of the birth record. The materials would explain a federal "Trump account," a 529 college savings plan, and an ABLE savings account for people with disabilities.

KS-2025-SB347.s: The bill would stop the secretary of state from appointing county election commissioners starting July 1, 2026. When a county election commissioner’s office becomes vacant, the county clerk would take over the job of running and overseeing elections in that county. Election records tied to that office would also be handed to the county clerk.

KS-2025-SB391.s: The bill would bar cities and counties from passing rules that require landlords to rent to people using housing vouchers or other housing aid. It would also stop local rules that limit how landlords can weigh a tenant's income source, credit, eviction history, property damage history, or criminal history when choosing renters. Any city or county rule like that adopted before July 1, 2026, would be void.

KS-2025-SB437.s: The bill would create a technical college funding task force in Kansas. The group would study a pilot funding plan that ties state money to results such as student progress, job placement, and credentials, and it would report its ideas to the Legislature by January 31, 2028. The task force would include technical college leaders and lawmakers' appointees, and it could ask for staff help and travel pay if approved.

KS-2025-SB74.s: For tax years 2025 through 2027, Kansas residents could get a tax credit for part of the cost of buying lockable gun and ammunition storage. The credit would equal 25% of the expense, up to $250 per taxpayer each year, and any extra over the tax due would be refunded.
